body:
Copyright protection has statutory limits

Copyright does not prohibit every use of protected material by another person. Section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957 identifies acts that do not constitute infringement when the relevant statutory conditions are satisfied.

These exceptions help balance the interests of creators with education, research, public discussion, access to information and other recognised activities.

Fair dealing under Section 52

Fair dealing permits certain limited dealings with copyright works without obtaining the copyright owner's authorisation.

Section 52(1)(a) recognises fair dealing with works other than computer programs for these purposes:

  • Private or personal use, including research.
  • Criticism or review, whether of the work itself or another work.
  • Reporting current events and current affairs, including reporting a lecture delivered in public.

The presence of an eligible purpose does not automatically make every amount or method of copying lawful. The dealing must be fair in its circumstances.

For example, quoting a limited passage for genuine criticism may fall within the exception. Republishing an entire commercially available textbook merely because the uploader describes it as educational does not automatically qualify.

Indian copyright law does not provide a universal rule that copying a fixed percentage, such as 10%, is always fair. The applicable exception and circumstances must be examined.

Educational and other specific exceptions

Section 52 includes other exceptions with their own conditions.

  • Instruction and examinations: Section 52(1)(i) covers reproduction of a work by a teacher or pupil in the course of instruction and certain uses involving examination questions and answers.
  • Computer programs: Section 52(1)(aa) recognises specified copying or adaptation by a lawful possessor for the supplied purpose and permitted backup purposes. Other software-specific exceptions also exist.
  • Libraries: non-commercial public libraries may electronically preserve works already held in non-digital form and make up to 3 copies of a book unavailable for sale in India for library use.
  • Accessibility: Section 52(1)(zb) provides specified exceptions for accessible-format use benefiting persons with disabilities. Accessible copies must be supplied on a non-profit basis, recovering only production costs.
  • Electronic transmission: transient or incidental storage purely in the technical process of electronic transmission or communication to the public is exempt.

The Act does not create an unrestricted permission for every school, library, software user or internet intermediary. Each exception has its own requirements.

Copyright and the internet

Digital technology allows works to be copied, stored, modified and transmitted rapidly. Because Section 14 includes electronic reproduction and communication rights, online conduct can involve copyright even when no printed copy is produced.

For example, uploading unauthorised copies of a protected commercial book to a public website may infringe reproduction and communication rights. Downloading a file for permitted private research, by contrast, must be examined in light of the applicable statutory exception and surrounding circumstances.

Material being freely accessible on the internet does not mean that it has entered the public domain. A creator may provide free access while retaining copyright.

Technological protection measures

Section 65A addresses circumvention of effective technological measures used to protect copyright rights. Its penal provision concerns circumvention undertaken with the intention of infringing those rights, subject to statutory exceptions.

Section 65B protects rights-management information against specified knowing and unauthorised removal, alteration and related dealings.

Rights-management information can identify a work, author, rights owner or conditions of use. These provisions are relevant to digital distribution, although not every technological circumvention or alteration is automatically an offence.

How long does copyright last in India?

Copyright duration depends on the category of work. The general periods below are derived from Chapter V of the Copyright Act.

CategoryOrdinary protection periodRelevant section
Published literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following the author's death22
Cinematograph films60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following first publication26
Sound recordings60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following first publication27
Government works where Government is first owner60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following first publication28

For joint-authored works covered by Section 22, the relevant death is that of the last surviving author. Special provisions apply to categories such as certain anonymous, pseudonymous and posthumous works.

Understanding the starting year

Suppose an author of a qualifying published literary work dies in 2020. The ordinary 60-year period begins on 1 January 2021 and runs through 31 December 2080.

For a cinematograph film first published in 2020, the ordinary 60-year period also begins on 1 January 2021. The calculation is based on publication rather than the death of the film's producer.

After copyright expires, the work's relevant protected expression ordinarily enters the public domain, allowing use without permission under that expired copyright. Separate copyrights in later adaptations or other incorporated material may still subsist.

Prelims focus

  • Section 52 contains statutory exceptions to copyright infringement.
  • Section 52(1)(a) concerns specified fair dealing, excluding computer programs from that particular clause.
  • Section 65A addresses intentional infringing circumvention of technological measures.
  • Section 65B addresses specified unauthorised dealings with rights-management information.
  • Section 22 generally provides the author's life plus 60 years, calculated from the following calendar year.
  • Trap: Cinematograph-film and sound-recording copyright terms are ordinarily calculated from first publication, not the producer's death.

[Sources: Copyright Act, 1957, Chapter V, Sections 22–29; Chapter XI, Section 52; Chapter XIII, Sections 65A–65B, Copyright Office, consulted 14 November 2026; Intellectual Property India, Basics of Copyright, consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Copyright: Fair Dealing, Digital Infringement and Duration

body:
Meaning and purpose of a trademark

A trademark is a sign capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person or business from those of others, subject to the requirements of the Trade Marks Act, 1999.

A trademark allows consumers to associate goods or services with a particular commercial source. This identification helps protect the goodwill built through consistent commercial activity.

The law also reduces unfair commercial confusion. If competing businesses use deceptively similar signs, consumers may mistakenly believe that their products have the same origin or are commercially connected.

What can function as a trademark?

A trademark may include a word, personal name, letters, numerals, logo, device, combination of colours, shape of goods or packaging, or a qualifying sound.

Indian law requires the sign to be capable of graphical representation and to satisfy the applicable distinctiveness requirements.

A business may register a distinctive word mark independently of the particular artistic style in which the word appears. A device or logo mark, by contrast, may protect a specified visual representation.

Distinctiveness is the central requirement

Distinctiveness means the ability of a sign to identify and distinguish the commercial source of goods or services.

The strength of distinctiveness varies according to the relationship between a sign and the goods or services concerned.

Inherently distinctive marks

An invented word that does not describe the goods is generally capable of being highly distinctive.

An ordinary word used for unrelated goods may also be distinctive. For example, a common natural-object word used as the name of a software service may distinguish its source rather than describe its function.

A suggestive mark may hint at a product characteristic without directly describing it. Such a sign can be distinctive where consumers must make a mental connection to understand the suggestion.

Descriptive and generic expressions

A directly descriptive expression ordinarily identifies a characteristic rather than a particular business. For example, the expression describing freshly baked bread may simply tell consumers what a bakery sells.

Under Section 9, certain descriptive marks may become registrable if they have acquired distinctive character through use before the application date, or are well-known trademarks before that date.

A generic term is the ordinary name of the goods or services themselves. It cannot ordinarily be monopolised as a trademark for those goods or services merely by one trader adopting it.

Absolute and relative grounds for refusal

The Trade Marks Act distinguishes major grounds on which registration may be refused.

  • Section 9, absolute grounds: includes lack of distinctiveness, specified descriptive or customary signs, deceptive signs and certain prohibited matter.
  • Section 11, relative grounds: addresses conflicts with earlier trademarks and specified earlier rights, including situations involving likelihood of confusion.

For example, a proposed mark may be inherently distinctive but still be refused because it conflicts with an earlier protected mark for relevant goods or services.

How trademark registration works

A proprietor generally begins by identifying the mark and the goods or services for which protection is sought.

  1. Search: examine existing marks to identify possible conflicts.
  2. Application: file the proposed mark for the relevant goods or services with the Trade Marks Registry.
  3. Examination: the Registry examines whether the legal requirements are satisfied.
  4. Publication: an accepted application is advertised, allowing any person to oppose registration by written notice and payment of the fee to the Registrar within 4 months from advertisement or re-advertisement.
  5. Registration: if the applicable requirements are completed and no successful opposition prevents registration, the mark is registered.

Goods and services are classified for registration purposes. A trademark registration concerns its specified goods or services and is subject to statutory qualifications; it is not an unlimited monopoly over a word in every commercial context.

Duration of trademark registration

Under Section 25, a trademark registration ordinarily lasts 10 years. It may be renewed for successive periods of 10 years by applying to the Registrar in Form TM-R and paying the applicable fee; an ordinary renewal application may be filed during the year before expiry.

Consequently, a trademark can remain registered for many decades. Unlike the maximum ordinary term for a registered industrial design, trademark registration has no single fixed maximum number of renewal periods under Section 25.

Trademark registration is renewable every 10 years. A trademark may also attract protection through qualifying prior use even without registration, but an unregistered proprietor cannot bring a statutory infringement action merely as an unregistered proprietor.

Prelims focus

  • The Trade Marks Act, 1999 governs trademark protection in India.
  • Section 9 concerns absolute grounds for refusal.
  • Section 11 concerns relative grounds for refusal.
  • Distinctiveness is central to trademark eligibility.
  • Section 25 provides a 10-year registration period with successive 10-year renewals.
  • Trap: A descriptive expression is not automatically distinctive merely because a business uses it.

[Sources: Trade Marks Act, 1999, Sections 2, 7, 9, 11 and 18–25, Intellectual Property India; Intellectual Property India, Basics of Trademarks, consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Distinctive commercial signs help consumers recognise the source of goods and services.

pictures.alt: Trademark distinctiveness rises from generic to invented marks; descriptive marks may qualify through acquired distinctiveness if statutory conditions are met.

title: Trademarks: Distinctiveness, Eligibility and Registration

body:
Why trademark protection is enforced

A trademark performs its commercial function when consumers can reliably distinguish the goods and services of different businesses.

Unauthorised use of an identical or deceptively similar sign may confuse consumers, interfere with the proprietor's rights and damage business goodwill. Indian law provides different legal routes depending on the trademark's registration status and the circumstances of use.

Infringement of a registered trademark

Trademark infringement is a statutory wrong involving unauthorised conduct prohibited by the Trade Marks Act in relation to a registered trademark.

Section 29 contains several infringement grounds. In ordinary confusion-based cases, the relevant considerations include the similarity of the signs, the goods or services involved and whether the statutory requirements concerning confusion or commercial association are satisfied.

For example, suppose a registered brand is used for packaged tea. Another trader begins selling tea under a deceptively similar name and packaging that is likely to cause consumers to associate it with the registered proprietor. Depending on the facts and statutory conditions, this may amount to trademark infringement.

Exact copying is not always necessary. Deceptive similarity may be sufficient under applicable provisions.

Passing off protects commercial goodwill

Passing off is a legal action that addresses a trader's misrepresentation of goods or services as those of another business, or as commercially connected with that business, when the required elements are established.

Section 27(1) prevents an infringement action based solely on an unregistered trademark. Section 27(2), however, preserves the right to bring an action for passing off.

The essential elements of passing off

A conventional passing-off claim involves 3 connected elements:

  • Goodwill: the claimant has an established commercial reputation or customer association in the relevant business.
  • Misrepresentation: the defendant's conduct is likely to mislead relevant consumers into believing that the defendant's goods or services originate from, or are connected with, the claimant.
  • Damage: the misrepresentation causes or is likely to cause damage to that goodwill.

For example, a local bakery may have developed goodwill in a distinctive trading name over many years. If another bakery adopts confusingly similar commercial presentation and thereby misleads customers, the first bakery may have a passing-off claim even without trademark registration, provided the required facts are established.

Infringement and passing off compared

PointTrademark infringementPassing off
Legal basisStatutory protection of registered marksProtection of commercial goodwill against misrepresentation
RegistrationRequired for the registered-mark infringement claimNot essential
Central inquiryWhether statutory infringement conditions are satisfiedGoodwill, misrepresentation and damage
Actual copyingExact copying is not always requiredExact copying is not always required

A business may possess both registration-based rights and goodwill-based rights. Accordingly, infringement and passing-off claims can sometimes arise from the same conduct.

Trademark dilution and reputation

Some trademarks possess a strong reputation extending beyond one product category. Their unauthorised use on unrelated goods may take unfair advantage of that reputation or damage the mark's distinctive character.

Section 29(4) addresses a particular situation involving use of an identical or similar sign for dissimilar goods or services where the registered mark has a reputation in India and the other statutory conditions are satisfied.

These conditions include use without due cause that takes unfair advantage of, or is detrimental to, the distinctive character or repute of the registered mark.

This is commonly discussed as dilution-related protection. Unlike ordinary confusion-based infringement, the statutory ground does not depend on showing the same likelihood of confusion between similar goods or services.

A famous or reputed trademark does not automatically prohibit every use of a similar expression. Section 29(4) requires its own statutory conditions to be satisfied.

Limits on trademark rights

Trademark protection must coexist with legitimate commercial communication and earlier rights.

  • Section 30: provides specified limits on registered trademark rights, including certain honest referential or descriptive uses.
  • Section 34: protects qualifying continuous prior use of a mark against interference by a later registered proprietor; that use must predate the registered proprietor's first use or registration for the relevant goods or services, whichever is earlier.
  • Descriptive use: a trader may legitimately describe the characteristics of goods without necessarily presenting another person's mark as its own commercial identifier.

Trademark registration therefore does not provide unrestricted control over every mention of a brand name.

Passing off in digital markets

Online trading can also involve trademark-related deception. A website, online storefront or advertisement may misleadingly present goods as originating from another business.

The legal issue depends on the use of the sign and the relevant statutory or passing-off requirements. Merely mentioning another business by name does not automatically establish infringement or passing off.

Prelims focus

  • Section 27(1) bars statutory infringement proceedings based on an unregistered trademark.
  • Section 27(2) preserves passing-off actions.
  • Section 29 deals with infringement of registered trademarks.
  • Passing off involves goodwill, misrepresentation and damage.
  • Section 29(4) provides specified protection for reputed registered marks in relation to dissimilar goods or services.
  • Trap: Passing off does not require trademark registration, but it does require proof of its legal elements.

[Sources: Trade Marks Act, 1999, Sections 27–30 and 34, Intellectual Property India, consulted 14 November 2026; Intellectual Property India, Basics of Trademarks, Protection Against Infringement and Unregistered Marks.]
